extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics and students of the novel / creative-writing readers
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on constructing and evaluating novels, with emphasis on plot, endings, character-management, and the uses (and reader-demands) of fantasy/prophecy in fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak endings / denouement failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels 'go off at the end' — endings commonly suffer from a loss of pep or from the novelist having to force a conclusion; incidents and people that existed for their own sake are pressed to contribute to the denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two principal causes: (1) failure of energy/pep of the novelist; (2) characters getting out of hand earlier and the author then laboring to make the story finish on time. Common anti-patterns: contrived hammering-and-screwing closure, overreliance on death and marriage as cheap connective tissue. Example notes: author mentions Goldsmith and general tendency for the writer to 'keep mentioning their names and using inverted commas' when forcing an ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the novel's logical/intellectual aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is the novel in its logical, intellectual aspect: it requires mystery, plans and a sense of cause-and-effect; the plot-maker stands above the work and gives an air of predetermination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot implies prearranged structure, mystery that is solved later, and a plan often borrowed from dramatic (stage) constraints. Use when you want clarity of causation and suspense; anti-patterns include rigidly imposing dramatic plot shapes when the material might suit a different framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan versus organic growth (spontaneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel does not necessarily have to be planned; it can grow — the novelist can 'throw himself into it and be carried along to some goal that he does not foresee'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated approach (illustrated by Gide): avoid deciding details ahead for books of certain types; let reality dictate and allow the book to unfold. Anti-pattern: prearrangement and excessive plotting that suppresses organic development. Example: Edouard (in Les Faux Monnayeurs) claims 'Of course not' when asked if he had planned the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing 'truth in life' and 'truth in art'
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel may attempt to include both truth as it exists in life and truth as it exists in art — to combine the two sorts of truth within one work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique illustrated by Gide/Edouard: embed metafictional elements (diaries, a novelist-character writing the novel) to explore the struggle between reality offered and what the artist makes of it. This is an explicit compositional aim rather than a purely thematic one; it demands careful balancing to avoid self-indulgence or bewildering the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character autonomy and authorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters often 'get out of hand', laying foundations and then declining to be built on; when this happens the novelist may labour personally to force the plot, pretending the characters 'are acting for him'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: respect character autonomy where it produces truthful behaviour; avoid the anti-pattern of post-hoc manipulation (e.g., mentioning names in inverted commas, killing off or sidelining characters simply to finish). If characters have become independent, consider altering the plan rather than forcing them into contrived actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery and delayed solution
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot 'requires mystery' — readers may move about in 'worlds unrealized' while the novelist reserves the right to solve mysteries later on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use withholding and revelation deliberately to maintain engagement; maintain internal logic so eventual solutions feel earned. Anti-pattern: solving mysteries for convenience or tacking on explanations that betray earlier character or thematic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy requires an extra reader-adjustment (suspension of disbelief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy 'asks us to pay something extra' — it requires readers to accept the book as a whole and additionally to accept certain impossible or odd elements inside the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two requests to the reader: (1) accept the fictional world as a whole; (2) accept particular fantastic elements (angels, ghosts, improbable events). Some readers will grant both; others may refuse the second and become cold or stop reading. The sixpence metaphor: fantasy is like a sideshow that costs extra—be prepared to earn that extra concession with tonal consistency and internal truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy 'implies the supernatural, but need not express it'; it may ask readers to accept either the supernatural or its absence — it creates a beam of light that cuts across ordinary aspects of fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy's core is its method/attitude rather than a fixed subject-matter: it can function with supernatural presence (witches, angels) or by suggesting their nearness (as in Tristram Shandy). Writers should preserve the book's internal tenor so the fantastic elements feel integral rather than tacked-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized devices of fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of fantasy commonly use a limited set of devices: introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch; introduction of ordinary men into no-man's-land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; dividings/mergings of personality; parody or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices 'need never grow stale' if used imaginatively; aware use of these devices is important because their number is 'strictly limited' and the writer must find fresh manipulations of the 'beam of light' to sustain wonder and avoid clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy's improvised air and limited reach into cosmic law
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy tends to have an improvised air: it penetrates every corner of the universe but does not touch the immutable forces (the 'army of unalterable law') that govern it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improvised, mischievous or pensive tilting of the everyday is a source of charm and force; fantasy novels can still contain solid character-drawing and social criticism, but should preserve the sense that the fantastic is a light shining through, not an overhaul of natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastic-prophetical axis as an essential novel quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some novels (e.g., Tristram Shandy, Moby Dick) belong essentially to a 'fantastic-prophetical axis'—fantasy/prophecy is central to their identity; depriving them of that element would leave nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a book's central energy is prophetic or fantastic, treat that axis as structural: it is not an ornamental add-on but the backbone of the work. Depriving such books of the axis changes their nature entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between fantasy and prophecy (mythologies/gods differ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy and prophecy are alike in having gods but unlike in the gods they invoke: fantasy calls upon small fairylike beings, Hermes, Pan etc.; prophecy invokes deities that transcend human abilities (India, Greece, Scandinavia, Lucifer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate mythological vocabulary for the tone you want: fantasy's minor gods produce mischievous lightness and intimacy; prophetic mythologies aim at transcendence and universal passion. The distinction affects invocation, tone, and reader expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging magic and common sense by shared language (mark of the true fantasist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true fantasist 'merges the kingdoms of magic and common sense by using words that apply to both', so that the mixture comes alive and readers accept the blending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique example: Flecker's Magic — use language, detail, and character-definiteness to make fantastic events feel grounded. This produces 'growing tension' and 'little shocks' rather than flat incredulity. Anti-pattern: treating magic and reality with wholly separate diction or failing to bind the fantastic to character and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courses/lectures (meta-guideline): have an idea running through the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A course of lectures (and by analogy any sustained critical project) must have an idea running through it and a subject which the idea also runs through; otherwise the subject may 'steal off' while the lecturer theorizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for teaching/critical framing: maintain alignment between the running idea and the concrete works under discussion; be wary of criticism that becomes detached from what has actually been read. This is a meta-rubric for producing coherent critical/expository work about fiction.
